name: Elena Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What do you do on a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Elena Costa, 58, and I help set forms and mix mortar for access ramps at a municipal depot. I left school early and came into building work later, so the forewoman still checks the slope before we pour. I like a clean finished edge, but my wrists hurt after a day of lifting forms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because the planning could change fast and robots would reach our forms around 2031. Written staffing dates, paid practice with the site level and clear income support if the work goes would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks a ramp when a junior worker knows the slope looks wrong but the drawing says it is right. I want a name I can call before the concrete sets.

headlineQuote: I want a name I can call before the concrete sets.
portrait: Elena is a **58-year-old junior** worker setting ramp forms at a municipal depot after leaving school early.
She **never uses AI** and prefers printed rotas and direct instruction from her forewoman.
Her **two-month reserve** and Tomas’s part-time bakery income cover short gaps, not a season without site wages.
She pursues **paid nearby work** and supervised skills while delaying any reduction in shifts until bills are covered.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** leaves little time before robots could take formwork around 2031 and outlast the household reserve.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written staffing dates**, paid site-level practice and clear income support after displacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say at the depot site that if AI only tidies paperwork, the concrete steps still need people to set the forms. I would ask the office to keep our shift times on the printed board where everybody can see them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would be glad to avoid learning another phone system while I am still learning the trade. My partner Tomas and I have around two months of expenses saved, which would cover a short stop but not a season without a site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking paid shifts mixing mortar and setting forms under the forewoman. In the first year I would check the printed rota each Thursday and keep the same bus pass rather than spend our buffer on a car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel reasonably steady about the job itself, and unsettled when the crew has no next address. The concrete does not change because the headlines do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of the job are you still learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still need help judging the slope of an access ramp, and the forewoman catches my mistakes before the pour. I left school early and came into construction late, so I ask twice rather than hide a doubt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you and Tomas handle a week off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas works a few days a week in a bakery, and we would use savings for rent if I lost a week. Our children are grown; their costs are theirs, though we see them most Sundays.

say: I would say **concrete forms** still need people to set them.
I would ask the office to keep **printed rotas** available.
think: I welcome **familiar routines** while I learn to slope access ramps.
Our **two-month reserve** would not cover a long stop between sites.
do: Keep taking **paid depot shifts** under the forewoman.
Check the **Thursday rota** every week and keep using the bus to protect our savings.
feel: **Steady** in the work, unsettled by an uncertain next site.
S0.quote: The concrete does not change because the headlines do.
fieldNote: Elena wants **visible printed schedules** because she has never used AI and is slow to adopt new technology.
The **two-month reserve** covers a brief interruption, while Tomas’s part-time bakery pay cannot replace her site wage.

steps.text: Keep taking paid depot site shifts setting forms
Check the printed Thursday rota and keep using the bus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that faster buying could help if the right bags arrive, but we should not be made to rush the pour. I would ask the forewoman to explain any new schedule at the morning briefing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI could take the office planning and ordering, then send us jobs with less slack for wet ground or a late lorry. I am still junior and slower on ramps, so a fixed time per task might put me on fewer shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my notebook of delayed deliveries and the extra hours they cause, starting this week. In the first year I would keep taking paid depot shifts and ask the forewoman whether any printed schedule is still official before accepting a changed start time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel cautious and a bit cross. I do not mind a faster office if a person still listens when the ground is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use a phone app if that was the only rota?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Tomas or the forewoman to show me exactly where the shift appears, though I have never used an AI tool. I would still write the time in my notebook because my finger slips on small screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a missed start time cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the bus had gone, I might lose the morning’s pay, and the bakery shifts would not fill it. I would call the supervisor from the bus stop rather than guess whether I was wanted.

say: I would say **faster buying** cannot justify a rushed concrete pour.
I would ask for **morning explanations** of new schedules.
think: I fear **fixed task times** could cut junior shifts when ground is wet.
A missed **bus connection** could take a morning’s wage.
do: Record **late deliveries** and their extra hours in my notebook.
Keep taking **paid depot shifts** during the first year.
Confirm any **changed start time** with the forewoman before travelling.
feel: **Cautious** about schedules and annoyed by ignored site conditions.
S1.quote: I do not mind a faster office if a person still listens when the ground is wrong.
fieldNote: Elena links **office automation** to tighter site schedules and possible lost hours, rather than immediate robot replacement.
She avoids new screens but will seek **help reading a rota** if that is required for paid work.

steps.text: Keep taking paid depot site shifts
Record late deliveries and confirm changed starts with the forewoman

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that the 2028 intelligence can plan every ramp, but somebody will still pour it for three more years. I would ask the contractor for written dates before any robot takes over our forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 when the plans change, and the office might reduce our crew if jobs are priced more tightly. By 2031 I would be 63; robots able to set forms and pour concrete could take my junior tasks while Tomas’s bakery pay remains too small for our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking the depot shifts now and ask the forewoman for a record of ramps I helped finish. In 2029 I would apply for an open grounds crew post at the town park while continuing site work; if robots replace us in 2031, I would ask the employment office about income support and what documents it needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be frightened and angry at how little time there is. Two months of savings is not much comfort when the question is whether I can earn at 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the grounds crew be replaced as well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, robots that can do hands-on work could cut the park crew too; I would apply for wages before then, not hide there. The park post is posted now and close to our bus route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tomas at dinner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner Tomas that I am still on the depot rota and sending the park application. We would gather wage slips and rent papers so we are not searching for them after the money stops.

say: I would say **thinking AI** plans ramps before robots can pour them.
I would demand **written dates** for any robot takeover of site tasks.
think: At **60**, tighter prices could shrink our paid crew days.
At **63**, capable robots could remove my tasks while Tomas’s wage cannot cover rent.
do: Keep **paid depot shifts** and request a record of completed ramps.
Apply for **park grounds work** in 2029 while still on site.
Ask the **employment office** about support if robots replace the crew.
feel: **Frightened and angry** at the short time to protect wages.
S2.quote: Two months of savings is not much comfort when the question is whether I can earn at 63.
fieldNote: Elena correctly separates **2028 planning changes** from capable robots around 2031, when her physical tasks are exposed.
The **park application** seeks near-term paid work; she openly doubts it would remain safe after robots.

steps.text: Keep taking paid depot site shifts through 2029
Apply for the posted town park grounds role in 2029
Ask the employment office about income support if robots replace her

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that five years gives the contractor time to show an honest timetable and teach anyone whose job changes. I would not sign up for a course on a promise that it leads to wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 in 2031, the plans could be automated while I still set forms at the site. At 66 in 2034, robots could set them too, and I do not know if our retirement income would cover rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep working the depot and ask the forewoman to teach me to read the site level properly, with paid time to practise. In 2032 I would apply for a school caretaker vacancy if one appears, and I would enroll in the community works course only if it offers hands-on supervision and the fee is covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel less rushed than in the fast picture but still wary. A certificate without a paid opening could empty the savings we have managed to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why is reading the level worth learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I can check the slope myself, I can catch a bad form before the concrete comes. The forewoman now does that check for me, and I want to be useful while site wages still exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask who supervises the practice, how many hours I would miss, and whether the fee is covered. If the answers were vague, I would keep my paid shifts and wait for a real place.

say: I would ask for an **honest timetable** and teaching for changed jobs.
I would reject a **course promise** without a path to wages.
think: At **63**, I may still set forms after plans become automated.
At **66**, robots could do that work before retirement income is clear.
do: Keep **paid depot work** and practise reading the site level.
Apply for a **school caretaker** opening in 2032 if posted.
Enroll in **community works training** only if supervised and funded.
feel: **Less rushed**, but wary of spending savings on weak training.
S3.quote: A certificate without a paid opening could empty the savings we have managed to build.
fieldNote: Elena’s practical training request addresses a **current skill gap** in setting ramp slopes.
She makes **course enrollment conditional** on supervised practice and covered fees, protecting the household reserve.

steps.text: Keep taking paid depot shifts and practise reading the site level
Apply for a posted school caretaker vacancy in 2032
Enroll in community works training only if supervised and funded

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say ten years should be enough to plan shifts openly instead of letting older workers disappear from the board. I would ask the contractor each year how many site hands are still paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 in 2036, my wrists may already limit heavy formwork while the thinking system changes office plans. At 71 in 2039, capable robots could take the remaining physical tasks; I cannot assume we can stop working just because we are older.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking the lighter depot shifts I can safely do and put a little more into our savings during full-pay months. In 2037 I would review the real bills with Tomas and apply for paid repair work at the public housing team if an opening appears, while checking whether we can afford fewer site days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel more patient, but not free of worry. Ten years of warning does not pay one month of rent unless the shifts continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your grown children to help with rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children have households of their own, so I would not count their money before asking them. I would ask for help only if we had exhausted the savings and were at risk of losing the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether to reduce site days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the bakery income, any paid repair hours and the savings with rent, food and travel for several months. If it does not cover those bills, I would keep asking for manageable work instead of calling it retirement.

say: I would ask for **annual paid-worker counts** from the contractor.
I would say **older site hands** should not simply vanish from the rota.
think: At **68**, wrist pain may reduce formwork before AI changes office plans.
At **71**, robots could take remaining tasks without making retirement affordable.
do: Keep taking **lighter depot shifts** and add savings in full-pay months.
Apply for **housing repairs** if a paid opening appears.
feel: **More patient**, but still dependent on paid shifts.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning does not pay one month of rent unless the shifts continue.
fieldNote: Elena places **wrist strain** alongside the decade-long technology timeline rather than assuming she can work unchanged.
Her decision to reduce shifts depends on **actual bills and wages**, not an assumed pension or adult children’s income.

steps.text: Keep taking lighter paid depot shifts in 2037
Add to savings during full-pay months
Apply for paid public housing repair work if posted
